“I’s gwine, Massa Will—indeed I is,” the negro answered at once—“mos’ reached de eend already.”

“Reached the end!” Legrand almost shrieked at this. “Are you telling me you are at the end of that branch?”

“Be at de eend soon, massa—o-o-o-o-oh! Lord hab mercy! what’s dis up here on de tree?”

“Well!” exclaimed Legrand in great delight, “what have you found?”

“Why, it’s noffin but a skull—somebody’s lef’ his head up in de tree, and de crows has eaten every scrap ob meat away.”

“A skull, is it!—very good—how is it secured to the branch?—what keeps it there?”

“True enough, massa; I mus’ look. Well, dis a mighty queer sarcumstance, I declare—dere’s a great big nail through de skull, a-fastening it to de tree.”

“Now then, Jupiter, follow my directions exactly—do you understand?”

“Yes, massa.”

“Attend, then—locate the skull’s left eye.”

“Hum! hoo! dat’s a good one! why, dere ain’t any eye lef’ whatever.”

“Confound your stupidity! Can you distinguish your right hand from your left?”

“Yes, I knows dat—knows it perfectly—it’s wid my lef’ hand I chops de wood.”

“Certainly! You are left-handed; and your left eye is upon the same side as your left hand. You can now, I presume, find the skull’s left eye, or the spot where its left eye formerly was. Have you got it?”

A lengthy silence followed. Finally the negro inquired,

“Is de skull’s lef’ eye on de same side as de skull’s lef’ hand, too?—for de skull ain’t got any hand at all—not a bit—nebber mind! I’s found de lef’ eye now—here it is! what mus’ I do wid it?”

“Lower the beetle through it to the full length of the string—but take care to keep hold of the string.”

“Dat’s done, Massa Will; putting de bug through de hole’s a mighty easy business—watch for him down dere!”

Throughout this exchange Jupiter himself remained entirely concealed; but the beetle he had lowered could now be seen at the string’s end, shining like a polished golden globe in the final beams of sunset, a few of which still dimly lighted the height where we stood. The scarabæus dangled wholly free of the branches, and would, if released, have dropped at our feet. Legrand at once picked up the scythe and used it to clear a circle some three or four yards across immediately below the insect. When this was finished, he directed Jupiter to release the string and descend from the tree.

All the young people were desperate to see Lyme. Captain Wentworth spoke of returning there himself; it was only seventeen miles from Uppercross, and although it was November, the weather was quite good. Louisa, in short, was the most enthusiastic of them all. Once she had decided to go, she had both the pleasure of getting her own way and her new conviction that standing by her decisions was a virtue to support her. She overcame every wish her father and mother expressed to postpone the visit until summer. So they were going to Lyme: Charles, Mary, Anne, Henrietta, Louisa, and Captain Wentworth.

Their first, thoughtless plan was to leave in the morning and return that night. Mr Musgrove, however, refused to agree for his horses’ sake; and once they considered it sensibly, they realized that a day in mid-November allowed little time to explore a new place after subtracting the seven hours the countryside made necessary for the journey there and back. They would therefore spend the night and were not expected home until dinner the following day. Everyone regarded this as a considerable improvement. Yet although they assembled at the Great House for a rather early breakfast and left precisely on time, it was well past noon when the two carriages began descending the long hill into Lyme and turned onto the even steeper street in the town itself. Mr Musgrove’s coach carried the four ladies, while Charles drove Captain Wentworth in his curricle. Clearly they would have barely enough time to look around before the daylight and warmth disappeared.

Once they had arranged their accommodation and ordered dinner at one of the inns, their next step was unquestionably to walk straight down to the sea. They had arrived too late in the year for any of the entertainment or variety Lyme could provide as a resort. The assembly rooms were closed, almost all the visitors had left their lodgings, and scarcely any families remained apart from those who lived there. Since the buildings themselves offer nothing to admire, a visitor’s attention turns to the town’s remarkable setting: its principal street seems almost to rush into the water; the walk to the Cobb follows the edge of the pleasant little bay, lively in the season with bathing machines and holidaymakers; and the Cobb itself has its old marvels and recent improvements. Beyond them lies the beautiful stretch of cliffs running eastward from the town. It would take a very unusual visitor to find no charm in Lyme’s immediate surroundings, nothing that made them want to become better acquainted with the place.

“Tom!”

There was no reply.

“TOM!”

Still no reply.

“Where can that boy have got to? You TOM!”

No reply came.

The old woman lowered her spectacles and surveyed the room above them; then she raised them and peered beneath. She hardly ever, if ever, looked through them for anything so insignificant as a boy. They were her ceremonial pair, her heart’s delight, made for “style” rather than use—two stove-lids would have served her sight as well. For an instant she appeared puzzled, then spoke, without fierceness, yet loudly enough to reach the furniture:

“Well, I reckon if I lay hands on you I’ll—”

She left the threat unfinished, for she was now stooping and jabbing beneath the bed with her broom, and needed her breath to give emphasis to the jabs. All she brought forth was the cat.

“I never saw the like of that boy!”

She walked to the open doorway, stood there, and gazed out through the tomato plants and “jimpson” weeds that made up the garden. Tom was absent. Accordingly she pitched her voice at an angle suited to carrying far and called:

“Y-o-u-u TOM!”

A faint sound came from behind. Turning, she caught a little boy by the loose cloth of his roundabout just in time to stop his escape.

“There now! I ought to ’a’ remembered that closet. What have you been doing inside?”

“Nothing.”

“Nothing! Just look at those hands. And your mouth, too. What’s that stuff?”

“I don’t know, aunt.”

“Well, I do. Jam—that’s what. I’ve told you forty times I’d skin you if you wouldn’t leave that jam alone. Give me that switch.”

The switch hung aloft—the danger was extreme—

“Oh! Look behind you, aunt!”

The old woman spun about, whisking her skirts away from danger. Instantly the boy bolted, clambered up the tall board fence, and vanished on its farther side.

Aunt Polly remained astonished for a moment, then let out a soft laugh.

“Drat that boy, will I never learn a thing? Hasn’t he fooled me often enough that way to make me watch him by now? But there’s no fools like old fools. You can’t teach an old dog new tricks, they say. Still, goodness knows, he never does it the same way two days running, and how’s anybody to guess what’s next? He seems to know exactly how far he can plague me before my temper rises; and he knows that if he manages to distract me a minute, or gets me laughing, it dies right down and I can’t give him one lick.”
